title: Chapter 108 — Merchandising Fundamentals
intro: Before you coach the salesperson, evaluate the selling environment. An empty display cannot generate sales. Sometimes the problem is not the person — it is the floor they are standing on.

sections.title: Check the Floor Before You Coach the Person
sections.content:
When a sales manager walks into a store, the first job is not to pull up a KPI report. It is to look at the floor.

Is the showroom clean? Are displays complete? Are there empty spaces where product should be? Is the floor easy to shop? Are products grouped logically? Can customers compare products easily? Does the layout support the sales process?

An empty display cannot generate sales. Poor merchandising creates obstacles before the salesperson even begins. If the environment is broken, no amount of coaching fixes the numbers.

This is something I see too often — managers jumping straight to individual performance metrics without first making sure the selling environment is set up for success.

sections.title: Floor Design Affects Closing Percentage
sections.content:
Floor design directly influences how well salespeople close. This is not opinion — it is math.

Wrong products displayed. Poor category organization. Difficult customer flow. Missing inventory. Weak merchandising. Displays that do not support comparison shopping. All of these make the salesperson's job harder before they say a single word.

When you are looking at refrigerators, are all the 33-inch models grouped together? Are all the 36-inch models together? Can you walk from the refrigerators to the ranges without crossing the entire sales floor? Can you move from brand to brand within a category without losing the customer?

The layout should support how people actually shop — which is by category and by comparison. If a customer wants to compare three different 36-inch French door refrigerators, they should be able to see them side by side. If they have to walk across the showroom to find the third option, you have already lost momentum.

sections.title: Manufacturer Goals vs. Retail Goals
sections.content:
This is one of the most important things you will learn about merchandising: manufacturers and retailers often have different objectives.

Manufacturers want exposure for their products. They want their brand featured prominently. They have specific display requirements and incentive programs tied to floor placement.

Retailers need to maximize profitability and meet the needs of their local market.

These are not always the same thing.

The right showroom is not necessarily the one the manufacturer recommends. It is the one that best fits your local demographics, customer psychographics, buying behavior, product mix, sales history, and margin opportunities.

Listening to the manufacturer without considering your own store demographics and the psychographics of your community can cost you a lot of sales. Manufacturers have their agenda. Retailers have theirs. You have to align them — not blindly accept one at the expense of the other.

Good retailers align manufacturer partnerships with their own business strategy rather than accepting every recommendation.

sections.title: The Right Product on the Right Floor
sections.content:
What product belongs on your showroom floor depends on many factors. It is not as simple as putting out whatever the manufacturer shipped.

Consider: what sells in your market? What price points match your customer base? What brands resonate locally? What are your highest-margin products? What categories are growing? What gaps exist in your current display?

The product on the floor should reflect your customer — not just your manufacturer's catalog. A store in a luxury neighborhood needs a different floor than a store in a value-driven market. A store near new construction needs different products than a store in an established area with aging appliances.

We will talk about this in more detail later in the program, but the key principle is this: the floor is a selling tool. If it is not set up to support how your customers shop, you are making every sale harder than it needs to be.

sections.title: Fill the Holes
sections.content:
You cannot sell empty spots. If a display position is empty — whether because inventory is late, a product was discontinued, or nobody updated the floor — that is revenue sitting at zero.

Every hole on the floor is a missed conversation. A customer walks by, sees nothing, and moves on. They do not ask 'what used to be there?' They just skip it.

Store managers should walk the floor daily and treat empty positions like emergency repairs. Get something in that spot. Get a temporary fill. Get a sign that says 'coming soon' at minimum. But never leave a hole and pretend it does not matter.

The presentation value of the store is the first thing a customer judges — before they talk to anyone, before they evaluate your product knowledge, before you even know they are there. If the floor looks incomplete, the first impression is already damaged.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
Before coaching individual salespeople on their closing percentage, evaluate the selling environment:

Are there holes on the floor? Are products positioned in a way that supports how customers shop? Are categories grouped logically for comparison? Can a customer flow through the showroom without confusion? Does the product mix reflect local demographics and buying behavior? Are manufacturer display recommendations aligned with the store's actual business strategy — or just accepted by default?

Sometimes the salesperson is not the problem. The store is. Fix the environment first. Then coach the person.
